subject: Modification indices: when are they "NA", and what to if suggested path makes model non-recursive?

messages.author: 598408fcf0cedf99
messages.subject: Modification indices: when are they "NA", and what to if suggested path makes model non-recursive?
parts:
Dear all,

I have two questions regarding modification indices:

1) What causes some modification indices to be "NA"? First I thought it had to do with variables containing NAs, but I even get some NAs for non-free parameters that only involve variables with no missing data.

For example in the model below, I get an NA for "herb.no.juvLH ~ omn", even though both variables have complete data and the parameter is non-free.

        modelA <- '
# regressions
        bpd ~ treat2 + treat3 + treat4 + pred
        plantNjul ~ treat2 + treat3 + treat4
        bpd.avheight ~ treat2 + treat3 + treat4
        plantpco1R ~ treat2 + treat3 + treat4
        herb.no.juvLH ~ bpd + bpd.avheight + plantNjul + plantpco1R
        omn ~   bpd + herb.no.juvLH + bpd.avheight + plantNjul + plantpco1R
        pred ~   herb.no.juvLH + omn + bpd.avheight + plantpco1R
# residual covariances
        plantNjul  ~~ bpd
        plantpco1R ~~ bpd
        plantpco1R ~~ plantNjul
        bpd.avheight ~~ bpd
        bpd.avheight ~~ plantNjul
        bpd.avheight ~~ plantpco1R
        '
fitA <- sem(modelA, data = shorteqvar, missing="ML",fixed.x=TRUE,estimator="MLR",group="veg")
summary(fitA, standardized=TRUE,rsq=TRUE)

2) A more general question: if a path X ~ Y is already in the model, and the modification index for Y ~ X is large, does this suggest to just add the Y ~ X path to the model, thus making the model non-recursive, or is it better to swap the X ~ Y path for the Y ~ X path, thus reversing the direction of the arrow in the original model?

Thanks.
M.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Modification indices: when are they "NA", and what to if suggested path makes model non-recursive?
parts:
You may get an NA if freeing the path would cause an identification problem, or would cause the whole model to fail identification.
     If the reciprocal path carries a large modification index, swapping one path for the other will not (generally) produce the same reduction in chi-square as promised by the modification index.  M.I.'s are always conditional on the model as currently specified, with current parameter estimates. M.I.'s only show you a lower bound on reduction of the chi-square--they don't advise you to change your model--they only show what will happen if you do.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Modification indices: when are they "NA", and what to if suggested path makes model non-recursive?
parts: 2) A more general question: if a path X ~ Y is already in the model, and the modification index for Y ~ X is large, does this suggest to just add the Y ~ X path to the model, thus making the model non-recursive, or is it better to swap the X ~ Y path for the Y ~ X path, thus reversing the direction of the arrow in the original model?

This can happen when you have indirect effects that don't fully capture the linear relationship between variables that are not directly related in the model.  If there are several such predictors that only indirectly affect an outcome, sometimes freeing an arrow in the other direction will be a way to increase multiple model-implied correlations with variables "upstream", but obviously that would make the model nonrecursive (without difficult-to-justify constraints).  General questions like this can be posted on SEMNET:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

But here is what I tell my students.  Modification indices give stupid advice all the time because they are calculated indiscriminately, without regard to any theoretical implications that are in the mind of the modeler, not the software.  Before inspecting modification indices, you should first inspect correlation residuals:

resid(fit, type = "cor")

Once you see which relationships are being inadequately accounted for by the model (e.g., which correlation residuals > .10 in magnitude), then YOU are smart enough to figure out which parameters should be considered for inspection (e.g., only one among X --> Y, Y --> X, or X <---> Y).  Once you have chosen which modification indices you will consider for inspection, just pay attention to those.
